source_note: Kampakis & Adamides (University College London), 'Using Twitter to predict football outcomes', undated manuscript circa 2014, 10 pages. First Twitter-based prediction study for association football (soccer): English Premier League, partial season 21 March - 11 May 2014. Three-model incremental design (Twitter-only / historical-statistics-only / combined) testing whether fan text adds information beyond historical statistics. Twitter pipeline: 1,975,614 fan tweets via open Streaming API for 20 teams; single-team hashtag assignment, multi-team discard, cross-sport nickname-collision filtering (Southampton Saints=NFL New Orleans Saints, Tottenham Spurs=NBA San Antonio Spurs); CMU ARK TwitterNLP POS filter (Adjective/Verb/Noun/Adverb/Interjection/Emoticon/Possessive), Porter stemmer, separate home/away unigram+bigram bags ranked by chi-square p-value + mutual information (1-35 features/side). Historical features: rolling pre-game averages (goals/corners/shots on target/fouls/yellow/red cards/squad age) + static market value/international players/EPL honours. Three-class outcome (home win/away win/draw), input x=[x_home,x_away]. Classifiers Naive Bayes/Random Forest/Logistic Regression/SVM (RBF/sigmoid/polynomial), leave-one-out CV, RF 100 seeds 10-1000 trees with OOB error; evaluated by accuracy + Cohen's kappa. Results: Twitter-only RF kappa 0.25/acc 65.6%, historical NB kappa 0.239/acc 58.9%, combined RF kappa 0.28/acc 69.6%; best bigrams via chi-square at ~11-15 features/side; combined beats individuals -> Twitter info not in simple stats. Volume skew (Liverpool 426,457 vs Fulham 15,530). Limitations: partial season, historical data hard to acquire (baseline fairness), majority-class accuracy inflation (kappa close), bigrams>unigrams (trigrams untested), nature of predictive info (fan emotion/news/injuries) not disambiguated. Extracted faithfully (not a derivative summary). Mostly qualitative/empirical: the only printed formulas (input-vector concatenation, feature-table symbols) extract garbled; input vector and Cohen's kappa reconstructed in labeled LaTeX and flagged here and in assumptions; remaining primitives are qualitative decision/processing heuristics with latex empty and breakdown_regime no_equation_domain. Domain football matches catalog (association football / soccer English Premier League social-media prediction). Directly relevant to GSE's complementary social-signal layer, entity-resolution/collision vetoes, venue-conditioned vocabulary, supervised feature selection, incremental-signal-value test, and chance-corrected evaluation. No sportsbook lines/spreads/totals/implied odds in source or lifted into GSE.

reasoning_traces.think: The retrocausal genealogy of this paper is the social-media-as-alternative-data turn in sports prediction. Stylianos Kampakis and Andreas Adamides of University College London, in an undated manuscript from around 2014, build on the demonstrated use of Twitter to predict elections, the stock market, box-office revenues and disease spread, and on the NFL-specific Twitter prediction of Sinha and colleagues and the TwitterPaul World Cup system, to ask whether the same signal works for association football, where no such study had yet been conducted. The work sits alongside the Bayesian historical-statistics lineage of Rue and Salvesen and Baio and Blangiardo, and tests whether fan-generated text carries information that those statistical models do not. The recursive theory of mind is the three-model incremental-value design. The authors construct a Twitter-only model, a historical-statistics-only model, and a combined model, so that the comparison answers not just whether Twitter predicts but whether it adds information beyond what historical statistics already supply. The Twitter pipeline retrieves about two million fan tweets through the open Streaming API over a partial Premier League season, assigns each tweet to exactly one team by hashtag, discards multi-team tweets, and filters cross-sport nickname collisions such as Southampton's Saints against the NFL and Tottenham's Spurs against the NBA; it then part-of-speech tags with the Carnegie Mellon ARK TwitterNLP tool, keeps content words and emoticons, stems with the Porter stemmer, and builds separate home and away bags of unigrams and bigrams ranked by chi-square and mutual information. Cross-layer veto adjudication is the classifier battery and its chance-corrected evaluation. Naive Bayes, random forests, logistic regression and support vector machines are compared under leave-one-out cross-validation, with the random forest averaged over one hundred seeds and ten to one thousand trees and its out-of-bag error used as the test estimate; performance is judged by accuracy and Cohen's kappa, the latter measuring improvement over random guessing. The Twitter random forest reaches a kappa of about zero point two five and accuracy of sixty-five point six percent, the historical Naive Bayes about zero point two four and fifty-eight point nine percent, and the combined random forest about zero point two eight and sixty-nine point six percent, with bigrams selected by chi-square and roughly eleven to fifteen features per side giving the best out-of-bag performance. The implementation invariants map directly onto GSE. The single-team hashtag assignment and the cross-sport nickname filtering are GSE's entity-resolution and collision vetoes for team-tagged social text; the separate home and away vocabularies are GSE's venue-role context split; the chi-square-plus-mutual-information ranking is GSE's supervised social-feature selection; the combined-beats-individuals result is GSE's orthogonal-signal evidence that fan text carries information absent from simple statistics; and the accuracy-versus-kappa divergence, where the Twitter forest may predict the majority class often, is GSE's caution against reading raw accuracy on imbalanced three-class outcomes. The empirical detail and the caveats together bound the claim. The corpus is exactly one million nine hundred seventy-five thousand six hundred fourteen tweets across twenty teams over the twenty-first of March to the eleventh of May 2014, with a pronounced volume skew — Liverpool at four hundred twenty-six thousand four hundred fifty-seven tweets against Fulham at fifteen thousand five hundred thirty — that reflects fan-base size and is a sampling caveat for per-team sentiment. The historical features mix rolling pre-game averages of goals, corners, shots on target, fouls and cards with static market value, squad age and honours, and the authors concede that acquiring historical data was difficult and that the weaker historical result may be a side-effect of the sources rather than a fair comparison. The related-work lineage and the feature engineering sharpen what the comparison actually tests. The authors position the study against Sinha's NFL Twitter n-grams, which matched or exceeded a statistics-only model, and against TwitterPaul's eighty-eight percent World Cup accuracy, while the historical side inherits the Bayesian generalized linear models of Rue and Salvesen and the hierarchical attack-defence goal models of Baio and Blangiardo; the historical feature set itself is modest, mixing six rolling pre-game averages and average squad age with static total market value, international-player count and a count of Premier League titles, runners-up finishes and doubles, so the historical baseline is a simple-statistics benchmark rather than a state-of-the-art Bayesian predictor. The bag-of-words is also venue-asymmetric by construction: a size-ten home bag plus a size-ten away bag means twenty total features at the x-axis value ten, and the same club carries different vocabulary at home than away, which is why the optimal eleven-to-fifteen features per side corresponds to roughly twenty-two to thirty total n-grams. The limitations close the account honestly. The experiment covers only part of a season, not a whole one, and cross-season transfer is left to future work; bigrams outperform unigrams, suggesting the information is more complex than single words capture, but whether trigrams help is untested; and crucially the nature of the predictive information — fan emotion, outcome discussion, or injury news absent from statistical models — is speculated but not disambiguated. The invariant for GSE is to treat Twitter-derived bag-of-words features as a complementary, venue-conditioned, entity-resolved signal layer whose incremental value over historical statistics is demonstrated by the combined model, while carrying the partial-season scope, the volume skew, the majority-class accuracy inflation, the historical-baseline fairness question, and the undisambiguated signal source as honest bounds on what the social features can claim.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: Social-media-as-alternative-data turn in sports prediction. Stylianos Kampakis, Andreas Adamides (University College London); undated manuscript ~2014, 10 pages. Builds on Twitter predicting elections (Tumasjan 2010), stock market (Bollen 2011), box-office (Asur-Huberman 2010), disease (Paul-Dredze 2011); NFL Twitter (Sinha 2013 arXiv:1310.6998 n-grams match/exceed stats), TwitterPaul 2010 World Cup (UzZaman 2012 up to 88%). First soccer application. Alongside Bayesian historical lineage Rue-Salvesen 2000, Baio-Blangiardo 2010. Tests whether fan text adds info beyond historical stats. No DOI/arXiv for this manuscript itself.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Three-model incremental design: Twitter-only / historical-only / combined (does Twitter add beyond stats). Twitter pipeline: ~2M fan tweets via open Streaming API, 21 March-11 May 2014 partial EPL season, exact 1975614 tweets/20 teams; single-team hashtag assignment, discard multi-team, filter cross-sport nickname collisions (Southampton Saints=NFL New Orleans, Tottenham Spurs=NBA San Antonio); CMU ARK TwitterNLP POS (keep Adj/Verb/Noun/Adv/Interjection/Emoticon/Possessive), Porter stemmer (Java), separate home/away unigram+bigram bags ranked by chi-square p-value + mutual information (1-35 features/side). Historical F1-6+F8 rolling pre-game averages (goals/corners/shots on target/fouls/yellow/red/squad age) + static market value/international players/EPL wins/runners-up/doubles. 3-class home/away/draw; input x=[x_home,x_away] (math garbled reconstructed).
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Classifiers Naive Bayes/RF/Logistic regression/SVM (RBF/sigmoid/poly kernels); leave-one-out CV; RF 100 seeds 10-1000 trees, OOB error as test estimate; accuracy + Cohen's kappa (kappa=(p_o-p_e)/(1-p_e), 0=random/1=perfect, formula reconstructed). Results Table 2: Twitter-only RF kappa 0.25±0.093 (0.047-0.389)/acc 65.6%±4.33% (56.3-74.7); historical NB kappa 0.239±0.075/acc 58.9%±5.97%; combined RF kappa 0.28±0.065/acc 69.6%±2.4% (64.4-74.7). Best bigrams via chi-square, ~11-15 features/side then falls. Majority-class caveat: Twitter RF high accuracy at expense of misclassification (kappa close to NB). Volume skew Liverpool 426457/Man United 416767 vs Fulham 15530/Swansea 15668 (~27x). Combined beats individuals -> Twitter info NOT in simple stats (orthogonal). Limitations: partial season not whole (future full + cross-season transfer), historical data difficult to acquire (weaker result may be source side-effect, not fair comparison), bigrams>unigrams (trigrams untested), nature of info (fan emotion/outcome discussion/injury news) speculated NOT disambiguated. Zero sportsbook lines lifted.

universal_lens: A University College London study tests whether fan tweets predict English Premier League outcomes by building Twitter-only, historical-statistics-only, and combined classifiers over a partial 2014 season, resolving tweets to single teams by hashtag while filtering cross-sport nickname collisions, selecting home/away bag-of-words n-grams by chi-square and mutual information, and evaluating with accuracy and Cohen's kappa; the Twitter random forest reaches about 65.6% accuracy and kappa 0.25, the combined model about 69.6% and kappa 0.28, and because the combination beats each individual the authors conclude Twitter carries information absent from simple statistics, while honestly bounding the claim with the partial-season scope, the fan-volume skew, the majority-class accuracy inflation, and the undisambiguated nature of the predictive signal.
gsi_mapping: GSI treats three-model incremental design (Twitter-only/historical-only/combined); Twitter 1975614 tweets/20 teams/21 March-11 May 2014 partial EPL via open Streaming API; single-team hashtag assignment + multi-team discard + cross-sport nickname-collision filter (Southampton Saints=NFL, Tottenham Spurs=NBA); CMU ARK TwitterNLP POS (Adj/Verb/Noun/Adv/Interjection/Emoticon/Possessive) + Porter stemmer + separate home/away unigram/bigram bags ranked chi-square p-value + mutual information (1-35/side); historical rolling pre-game averages (goals/corners/shots on target/fouls/yellow/red/squad age) + static market value/internationals/EPL honours; 3-class home/away/draw, x=[x_home,x_away] (garbled reconstructed); classifiers NB/RF/LR/SVM (RBF/sigmoid/poly), leave-one-out CV, RF 100 seeds 10-1000 trees OOB; accuracy + Cohen's kappa=(p_o-p_e)/(1-p_e) (reconstructed); Twitter RF kappa 0.25±0.093/acc 65.6%±4.33%, historical NB 0.239/58.9%, combined RF 0.28±0.065/69.6%±2.4%; best bigrams chi-square ~11-15/side then falls; majority-class accuracy inflation (kappa close to NB); volume skew Liverpool 426457/Fulham 15530 (~27x); combined beats individuals -> Twitter info not in stats; limitations partial season/historical-data difficulty (baseline fairness)/bigrams>unigrams (trigrams untested)/info nature (fan emotion/news/injuries) not disambiguated; mostly qualitative, input vector + kappa reconstructed.
gse_mapping: GSE lifts the single-team hashtag assignment and cross-sport nickname-collision filtering as its entity-resolution and collision vetoes for team-tagged social text, the separate home/away bags-of-words as its venue-role-conditioned vocabulary, the chi-square-plus-mutual-information n-gram ranking as its supervised social-feature selection, the Twitter/historical/combined incremental design as its orthogonal-signal marginal-value test (combined beats individuals -> fan text carries info absent from simple statistics), the Cohen's-kappa chance-corrected evaluation as its better-than-random metric with the majority-class accuracy-inflation caution, and the rolling-versus-static historical feature split as its time-varying covariate discipline; treats the fan-volume skew as a per-team sentiment sampling caveat and carries the partial-season scope, the historical-baseline fairness question, the bigram-over-unigram complexity finding, and the undisambiguated predictive-signal nature (fan emotion versus outcome discussion versus injury news) as honest bounds; all outputs are social-text-derived outcome probabilities, never sportsbook lines.
